headline: Hundreds of people in Taiwan legally changed their names to include the word 'salmon' after a sushi chain promised free meals to anyone whose ID card said so.
reveal: Real. Taiwan, March 2021: 331 people took part. The interior ministry begged them to stop, since everyone gets only three name changes. A year later, some were still stuck being Salmon.

sources.title: Legislators debate name-change limits after 'salmon chaos'
Taiwan pleads with citizens not to change name to 'Salmon'

author: claude

headline: A government language office warned an Italian restaurant that its menu broke the law because it contained too many Italian words, including the word 'pasta'.
reveal: Real. Montreal, 2013: 'Pastagate'. Quebec's French-language watchdog later admitted it had been overzealous, and its head resigned within weeks.

sources.title: Language watchdog admits being overzealous on word pasta on menu
'Pastagate' official resigns in Quebec

author: claude

headline: Police in Ireland hunted a serial traffic offender with more than 50 different addresses, until someone realised his 'name' meant driving licence in Polish.
reveal: Real. Ireland, revealed in 2009. Officers had been copying 'Prawo Jazdy' off Polish licences as the driver's name. An internal memo called it quite embarrassing.

sources.title: Dictionary helps crack case of notorious Polish serial offender
Irish cops tripped up by Prawo Jazdy dragnet

author: claude

headline: A mayor in southern Italy signed an official decree forbidding the residents of his ageing village from getting sick, with higher taxes for anyone who neglected their health.
reveal: Real. Sellia, Calabria, 2015. Population 537, most of them over 65. The decree came with check-ups at a new health centre. Enforcement is presumably tricky.

sources.title: Calabrian village 'bans dying'
Small Italian town in Calabria bans dying, threatens higher taxes

author: claude

headline: A country's newly appointed minister in charge of cybersecurity told parliament he had never used a computer in his life, because his staff had always done that for him.
reveal: Real. Japan, 2018. He also seemed unsure what a USB drive was. One commentator joked that no hacker could ever steal his data.

sources.title: Japan's new minister of cybersecurity has never used a computer
'I've never used a computer,' says Japan's new cybersecurity minister

author: claude

headline: An entire country became one or two years younger overnight when a new law took effect, scrapping its traditional way of counting people's ages.
reveal: Real. South Korea, 28 June 2023. Under 'Korean age', babies were one at birth and everyone aged a year every 1 January, so a December baby could be two within days.

sources.title: South Koreans become a year or two younger as traditional way of counting age scrapped
South Koreans get younger as traditional age system dropped

author: claude

headline: A European country made it illegal to keep just one guinea pig, ruling the animals are too social to live alone, and rent-a-guinea-pig services soon followed.
reveal: Real. Switzerland's 2008 animal-welfare rules. When one pet dies, owners can rent a companion for the survivor instead of breaking the law.

sources.title: Rent a guinea pig in Switzerland
QuickCheck: Is it illegal to own just one guinea pig in Switzerland?

author: claude

headline: A German state repealed an old beef-labelling law and, in doing so, wiped out what linguists considered the longest genuine word in the German language.
reveal: Real. 2013. Farewell to the 63-letter Rindfleischetikettierungsüberwachungsaufgabenübertragungsgesetz, made obsolete when the EU dropped a cattle-testing rule. Germans can now breathe.

sources.title: Law change kills Germany's longest word
European Union regulations spell end for Germany's longest word

author: claude

headline: A tiny Austrian village voted to officially change its name after decades of tourists posing for photos at its road sign, and repeatedly stealing it.
reveal: Real. On 1 January 2021, Fucking, Upper Austria, became Fugging. The sign had already been set in concrete to stop thefts.

sources.title: Austrian village of F**king renames itself Fugging after unwanted attention
Austria bids farewell to Fucking after a millennium of misunderstandings

author: claude

headline: A farmer in India spent 18 years trying to convince the government he was alive after a relative bribed an official to register him as dead and took his land.
reveal: Real. Uttar Pradesh, 1976 to 1994. He added 'Mritak' (deceased) to his name, founded an association for the officially dead and later won an Ig Nobel prize.

sources.title: 'Dead' fight for life in UP
India's land of the living dead

author: claude

headline: A judge was asked to decide whether a burrito counts as a sandwich, and ruled that it does not, citing a dictionary and sworn testimony from a chef.
reveal: Real. Massachusetts, 2006. A bakery chain's lease banned rival sandwich shops from its mall, so it tried to block a burrito restaurant. The ruling came down to two slices of bread.

sources.title: Panera loses lawsuit to Qdoba over lease issue
Massachusetts judge settles dispute by ruling burrito is not a sandwich

author: claude

headline: A European country went 541 days without forming a government after an election, setting a world record, while daily life carried on more or less as normal.
reveal: Real. Belgium, 2010 to 2011. A caretaker government kept the lights on, and some Belgians celebrated passing the previous record with parties.

sources.title: Longest time without a government in peacetime
Belgium marks 'political record'

author: claude

headline: Rules that limited how much a top-grade cucumber was allowed to bend, no more than 10mm for every 10cm of length, were officially scrapped after two decades.
reveal: Real. European Union, July 2009. Marketing standards for 26 fruits and vegetables went. The agriculture commissioner welcomed back the curved cucumber and the knobbly carrot.

sources.title: Ugly fruit and vegetables return
Europe in a pickle over rules for crooked cucumbers

author: claude

headline: Parents fined for failing to register their son's name tried to call him a 43-character string of consonants ending in 11116, which they said was pronounced 'Albin'.
reveal: Real. Sweden, 1996. The court rejected it. Their next attempt, the single letter 'A', also pronounced Albin, was rejected too.

sources.title: An Apple by any other name
Nutella, Smelly Head and other names you can't call your child

author: claude

headline: A national terminology commission officially replaced the word 'hashtag' in all government documents with a home-grown term meaning 'sharp word'.
reveal: Real. France, 2013: the hashtag became the 'mot-dièse'. Critics pointed out that a dièse is the musical sharp sign, which slants the wrong way.

sources.title: Mon Dieu! A 'hashtag' is now a 'mot-dièse' in France
France bins Twitter's 'hashtag' for Gallic word

author: claude

headline: A government published its list of baby names rejected by officials, including a full stop, '4Real', 'Mafia No Fear' and 'Lucifer'.
reveal: Real. New Zealand, 2013. Names can't be offensive, absurdly long or sound like a title, which is why 'Justice' was the most-rejected name of all.

sources.title: '4Real'? New Zealand reveals banned baby names
Banned babies' names list updated in New Zealand

author: claude

headline: A national broadcasting regulator discouraged television dramas about time travel, saying they disrespected history and lacked positive thoughts and meaning.
reveal: Real. China, 2011. Shows about modern people slipping back into imperial courts had become huge hits. The guidance came out on 1 April and was not a joke.

sources.title: China bans time travel
China bans time travel films and shows

author: claude

headline: A government formally turned down a citizens' petition to build a planet-destroying space station, citing the cost and saying it 'does not support blowing up planets'.
reveal: Real. United States, 2013. More than 34,000 people signed. The White House reply put the price at over $850 quadrillion and noted a single pilot could destroy the thing anyway.

sources.title: White House responds to Death Star petition
No 'Death Star' for U.S. military, White House says

author: claude

headline: A national weather agency spent about $220,000 on a rebrand, then asked journalists to stop using its well-known nickname in the middle of a flood crisis.
reveal: Real. Australia's Bureau of Meteorology, 2022. It hadn't reserved its new social media handles, which other people grabbed first. Two days later it said everyone could call it whatever they liked.

sources.title: 'It's ridiculous': Bureau of Meteorology's rebrand racked up $220k bill
The Bureau of Meteorology reneges on rebrand after online roasting

author: claude

headline: An exam-board clerk told auditors that 36 million in cash missing from her office vault had been swallowed by a mysterious snake.
reveal: Real. Makurdi, Nigeria, 2018: about $100,000 in naira. The anti-corruption agency tweeted that it shows no mercy for money-swallowing snakes. She later denied blaming the snake.

sources.title: Nigerians react as snake is blamed for $100,000 missing state funds
JAMB clerk: I never said snake swallowed it

author: claude

headline: Police in an Indian state with a total ban on alcohol said rats had drunk most of the confiscated liquor in their storerooms, roughly 900,000 litres.
reveal: Real. Bihar, 2017. Officers said the rodents gnawed through the bottle caps. A senior officer responded by ordering breathalyser tests for his own staff.

sources.title: Rats drink 900,000 litres of alcohol in Bihar: Police
'Rats drank nearly 1 million litres of confiscated alcohol in India's Bihar'

author: claude

headline: A government declared victory in its 'war on floppy disks' after scrapping more than 1,000 regulations that still required them for official paperwork.
reveal: Real. Japan, June 2024. The digital minister announced the win himself. One rule, about vehicle recycling, still needed a floppy. Next on his list: fax machines.

sources.title: Japan's digital minister declares victory against floppy disks
Japanese gov celebrates demise of the floppy disk

author: claude

headline: A country held a national raffle for its unwanted presidential jet, except the winners didn't get the jet, just cash, and the plane stayed parked in its hangar.
reveal: Real. Mexico, September 2020. A hundred winning tickets shared about $95 million in prize money. The Boeing 787 was still pictured on every ticket and still unsold.

sources.title: Mexico to raffle off huge presidential jet, sort of
Mexico holds symbolic raffle for unwanted presidential jet

author: claude

headline: A woman in Spain registered herself at a notary's office as the legal owner of the Sun and announced plans to charge everyone who used it.
reveal: Real. Galicia, 2010. She argued the space treaty stops countries, not people, from claiming stars. She later sued an auction site for blocking her sales of plots on the Sun.

sources.title: Spanish woman claims ownership of the Sun
Spaniard sues eBay over right to sell the Sun

author: claude

headline: A 19-year-old paid about £10 to legally change his name to a 13-word sentence naming six comic-book superheroes and claiming he was faster than all of them combined.
reveal: Real. Glastonbury, England, 2008. His legal name: Captain Fantastic Faster Than Superman Spiderman Batman Wolverine Hulk And The Flash Combined. He said he wanted to be unique.

sources.title: Teen's 'fantastic' new name super-long
Teen's 'fantastic' new name

author: claude

headline: A court in Paraguay ruled that a sword duel between two neighbours over a fence had been legal, because both men were registered blood donors.
reveal: Made up, and a famous internet myth. Paraguay never allowed duels for blood donors. Its neighbour Uruguay really did tolerate duelling between 1920 and 1992, though.
author: claude

headline: A municipal office in Germany rejected a man's planning application for a garden shed because the drawing had been submitted in pencil rather than ink.
reveal: Made up. Plausible enough that several German readers just nodded.
author: claude

headline: Japan's tax agency faxed 14,000 businesses asking them to switch to email for all future correspondence, and requested that they confirm by fax.
reveal: Made up. Japan really did fight a long war on floppy disks, though.
author: claude

headline: A council in England spent two years and £40,000 deciding whether a roundabout with a single tree on it legally counted as a public park.
reveal: Made up. The tree declined to comment.
author: claude

headline: A county clerk in Ohio refused to issue a marriage licence because the groom's legal middle name was a single exclamation mark.
reveal: Made up. Punctuation names do get rejected around the world, but this wedding never happened.
author: claude

headline: French inspectors fined a bakery for selling baguettes two centimetres shorter than the length printed on its price board.
reveal: Made up. Though France really does regulate what may legally be called traditional bread.
author: claude

headline: Brazil's electoral court rejected a council candidate whose chosen ballot name was just a 14-digit phone number, ruling it 'advertising, not a name'.
reveal: Made up. Brazilian ballot names are wild, but not this wild yet.
author: claude

headline: An Australian council told a farmer he needed a building permit for his scarecrow because, at 2.6 metres, it exceeded the height limit for a garden structure.
reveal: Made up. The crows remain unregulated.
author: claude

headline: Dutch officials ruled that a houseboat painted to look like a brick house still legally counted as a boat and ordered its owner to mount a lifebuoy by the front door.
reveal: Made up. A lifebuoy by the front door would still be good advice in the Netherlands.
author: claude

headline: A district office in Seoul granted honorary residency to a 40-year-old vending machine after neighbours petitioned to stop it being removed.
reveal: Made up. A beloved vending machine is very believable; the paperwork is not.
author: claude

headline: Taiwan's household registration office rejected a man's request to change his surname to all 26 letters of the English alphabet, written in order.
reveal: Made up. Taiwan's real name-change chaos involved salmon.
author: claude

headline: A railway office in India stopped a clerk's salary for 11 years because his attendance register said 'on leave', even though he came to work every day.
reveal: Made up. Indian bureaucracy has produced stranger, and true, cases of people declared dead.
author: claude

headline: A man in Mexico legally changed his name to his home Wi-Fi password so he would never forget it, then had to change both after friends kept logging on.
reveal: Made up. Please do not try this.
author: claude

headline: A Canadian province issued a fishing licence to a pet goldfish after its owner applied online as a joke and the form was approved automatically.
reveal: Made up. Automated forms have approved sillier things, but not this one.
author: claude

headline: Irish officials listed a sheep as a member of a household after its farmer filled in the national census form for 'everyone who slept here last night'.
reveal: Made up. The sheep would have had to list its occupation.
author: claude

headline: South Africa's traffic department issued a speeding ticket to a parked car, recording its speed as 0 km/h in a 60 zone.
reveal: Made up. Camera glitches are real; this one isn't.
author: claude

headline: Auditors in Egypt found that a camel had been listed as a full-time employee of a museum for six years, with its salary paid into its owner's account.
reveal: Made up. Payroll ghosts are common worldwide, but they are usually human.
author: claude

headline: Kenya's parliament spent an afternoon debating whether a goat could be accepted as collateral for a government small-business loan.
reveal: Made up. Many Kenyan farmers would argue a goat is better collateral than most.
author: claude

headline: Spain's postal service returned a letter to its sender because the address had been written as a rhyming poem, which a sorting office said it could not process.
reveal: Made up. A real Spanish post office would probably have enjoyed it.
author: claude

headline: Argentina's passport office rejected an applicant's photo because his moustache extended beyond the frame, asking him to trim it or resubmit.
reveal: Made up. Passport photo rules are strict everywhere, but nobody has been asked to trim for one. Yet.
author: claude
